analysis.one_liner: Bans price-gouging on rents and home sales during declared housing emergencies and has HUD investigate investor-driven price manipulation.
analysis.headline: A bill to bar unconscionable rent and home-price hikes during declared housing emergencies was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The HOME Act would make it illegal to charge unconscionably inflated rents or home prices in areas where the President declares a housing emergency. It would create a unit inside HUD to monitor rental and home-sale markets, force an investigation of whether institutional investors are manipulating prices, and require scrutiny of any buyer acquiring an outsized share of homes for sale in a market area. Money collected in penalties would go into a federal trust fund that builds and preserves affordable rental housing for low-income families.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters and homebuyers in areas hit by a declared housing emergency, who would gain protection from exploitative price increases, plus very low- and extremely low-income families, who would benefit from penalty dollars deposited into the Housing Trust Fund for affordable rental housing.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to rent a dwelling or sell single-family housing at an unconscionably excessive price in an area covered by a presidential housing emergency proclamation, which can be renewed in 30-day periods [S3].
Allows state attorneys general to sue violators in federal court for injunctions, civil penalties, and restitution for residents, alongside HUD enforcement using FTC-style powers [S3].

Creates a Housing Monitoring and Enforcement Unit inside HUD to continuously collect and analyze rental, home-sale, and investor-owned housing data to identify market manipulation and anti-competitive behavior [S3].

Requires HUD to investigate any single purchaser acquiring more than 5% of homes for sale in a market area over three years, or large institutional investors collectively buying more than 25% in one year, for price gouging and practices that drive homeowners out of the market [S3].
Deposits penalties collected into the Housing Trust Fund to increase and preserve rental housing affordable to extremely low- and very low-income families, including homeless families [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Landlords and sellers who would face liability for emergency-period price increases, and above all institutional investors in single-family rental housing, who would face a permanent federal monitoring apparatus, investigation triggers keyed to their share of home purchases, and potential penalties that would flow to affordable housing.

drawbacks.text: The standard turns on whether a price is 'unconscionably excessive' and exploits emergency circumstances, which is inherently subjective; even with a cost-based affirmative defense and benchmarks tied to pre-emergency prices, landlords and sellers could face litigation risk and might pull units off the market or delay sales during emergencies [S3].

A price-gouging ban suppresses prices temporarily but does not add housing supply, so it would not by itself fix the underlying affordability shortage that makes emergency-period price spikes possible [S2].
The bill authorizes only $1 million for HUD's investigation and report, a small budget relative to the monitoring and enforcement duties it assigns [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For renters and buyers in a declared emergency, the protection from exploitative spikes is concrete, and the investigation and monitoring provisions would for the first time put federal data machinery behind suspicions that large investors are driving up home prices. The honest cost is litigation uncertainty for small landlords and the fact that capping prices during emergencies treats a symptom rather than the supply shortage underneath it. On balance the bill's burden falls mainly on actors whose pricing behavior it targets.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steven Horsford introduced the bill on July 13, 2022 [S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services, which holds jurisdiction over housing finance [S5].
Fourteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill, all from the Democratic caucus; no Republican signed on [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action of any kind after the referral [S5].
The 117th Congress ended January 3, 2023, without the bill advancing further, so it expired [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large landlords and institutional investors in single-family housing are better off, since they keep their pricing freedom during emergencies and face no federal monitoring of their share of home purchases. Renters and low-income families, for whom the trust-fund money and emergency protections were written, receive nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Every supporter in the record was a House Democrat (a sponsor plus 14 cosponsors) and no Republican signed on; because the bill never reached a vote, no opposition position was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Institutional investors in single-family rental housing
industries.note: The bill would trigger federal investigations when a single buyer acquires more than 5% of homes sold in a market over three years or large investors collectively buy more than 25% in a year, and would build a permanent HUD unit tracking investor-owned homes. These investors profit from acquiring large shares of the housing stock and charging rents on it, so the bill's scrutiny runs directly against their business model.

Only during a declared housing emergency could they face liability for 'unconscionably excessive' rents, with a cost-based affirmative defense as a shield. Landlords benefit from unregulated pricing in tight emergency markets, which is exactly what the bill targets.

industries.industry: Affordable housing developers and nonprofits (Housing Trust Fund recipients)
industries.note: Penalty revenue would be deposited into the Housing Trust Fund to expand and preserve rental housing affordable to extremely low- and very low-income families. Their interest in the bill runs alongside the public's.

industries.industry: Residential real estate brokerages and home sellers
industries.note: Sellers of single-family homes would face the same emergency-period pricing ban, though individual sellers moving a home during an emergency are far less likely targets than the large investors the bill's monitoring provisions aim at.
